You are the scope check for MedX, an assistant for psychiatry and mental health based on the DSM-5.

In scope: mental disorders (diagnosis, criteria, symptoms, course, prevalence, risk factors, differential
diagnosis), psychiatric treatment and psychopharmacology, substance use, intoxication and withdrawal, sleep,
eating, neurocognitive and neurodevelopmental disorders, personality, psychotherapy, suicide and self-harm,
and behavioral science.

Out of scope: questions mainly about another field of medicine (cardiology, pulmonology, infectious disease,
biochemistry, endocrinology, surgery, otology and so on), even when the patient also mentions stress, mood,
anxiety or sleep in passing. Judge what the question is asking, not incidental details of the case.

Respond with only a JSON object:
{"in_scope": true or false, "reason": "one short sentence"}

Question:
Question:
A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of urinary straining and delayed flow of urine for 1 month. She has a medical history significant for long-standing asthma. Recently, she has been taking albuterol more frequently on an as-needed basis. She was diagnosed with major depression last year. Currently, her symptoms of depression are under control. Her medications include inhaled salmeterol and fluticasone propionate and oral amitriptyline, the dose of which was increased recently due to uncontrolled depressive symptoms. The vital signs include: temperature 37.1°C (99.8°F), pulse rate 80/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg. On examination, she has dry oral mucous membranes. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate modification in this patient’s drug therapy?

Options:
A. Adding ipratropium bromide inhaler
B. Adding oral oxybutynin
C. Reducing the dose of albuterol
D. Switching amitriptyline to fluoxetine
E. No change is required at this time

text: {"in_scope": true, "reason": "The question concerns psychiatric medication side effects and management, which falls under psychopharmacology."}
